section_structure.heading: Untitled introduction + abstract/SUMMARY
section_structure.summary: Opens from the Bekker passage Rhet. III.1 1404a11 where Aristotle, treating lexis, writes ἀλλ' ἅπαντα φαντασία ταῦτ' ἐστὶ καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν. Modern translators (Cope 'fancy'/'mental presentation, mere copy without reality'; Freese 'mere outward show'; Kennedy 'outward show'; Roberts 'fanciful'; Rapp 'reiner Anschein') near-unanimously render phantasia here pejoratively, leading Green (2000:158) to remark that 'I cannot find a modern translation that takes the word phantasia seriously.' González frames the article as a corrective: a psychological reading of phantasia in Rhet. III.1 is to be defended. The argument unfolds in four stages: (1) summarize the consensus rationale; (2) present evidence for a psychological reading; (3) survey phantasia across Aristotle's oeuvre; (4) draw implications for the rhetorical task. Cites Baldwin 1924 and Labarrière 1994 as the rare dissenters from the consensus. Programmatic note on 'psychological': not mere mental-representation-talk but a faculty of the human psykhē mediating between sense-perception and the higher cognitive faculties (memory, hope, doxa, hypolēpsis).

section_structure.heading: The Modern Consensus and Its Rationale
section_structure.summary: Locates the consensus in views about the lexis/hypokrisis relationship. The standard reading marginalizes hypokrisis as morally objectionable and ties phantasia exclusively to that objectionable hypokrisis, so that phantasia inherits hypokrisis's pejorative cast as 'mere show' or 'ostentatiousness.' González dissents: Aristotle never fully sidelines hypokrisis, and if hypokrisis is open to abuse, so are lexis and rhetoric as a whole; therefore phantasia is not the outcome or instrument of self-interested manipulation but belongs to ordinary perceptual-cognitive processing, abusable yet necessary. Reads 1403b18-22 on the order of business (pisteis → lexis → hypokrisis) and argues that at 1403b35-36 the proper subject becomes τὸ περὶ τὴν λέξιν, broader than hypokrisis; hypokrisis is a subordinate division of lexis but not a parenthesis. Construes the 1404a1-12 passage: τῆς πραγματείας τῆς περὶ τὴν ῥητορικήν as wholly πρὸς δόξαν; ostensibly admits lexis only ὡς ἀναγκαίου (necessary expedient); δίκαιον is 'to contend with the facts themselves'; ἀλλ' ὅμως μέγα δύναται διὰ τὴν τοῦ ἀκροατοῦ μοχθηρίαν. The φορτικόν of 1403b36 is paired with καλῶς ὑπολαμβανόμενον (which Cope renders 'rightly so considered' but which González — following Vettori 'recte ponderatum' — wants softer: 'when properly understood'). Sketches how the rhetoric/geometry contrast at 1404a12 has been read to license the negative reading of phantasia: rhetoric concedes phantasia because the audience is corrupt; geometry does not. Closes by listing the apparent reasons for the consensus: appeals to mokhthēria and phortikon imply censure; lexis is by Aristotle's own concession a 'necessary expedient' not pursued for its own sake; outside ἀπόδειξις is περίεργα; and the tight tie of δηλῶσαι to conceptual clarity (1404a10) makes the bulk of stylistic analysis look like external show.

section_structure.heading: Questioning the Consensus
section_structure.summary: Mounts the positive case. (i) The consensus inherits a Platonist anti-rhetorical bias; Aristotle's via media is more pragmatic. (ii) Mokhthēria and phortikon are best read not as inherent in lexis but as effects of the interplay between unprincipled orator and uncultivated audience (parallel: Poetics 26 on φορτική mimesis as dependent on θεαταί). (iii) The opposition πρὸς ἀλήθειαν vs. πρὸς δόξαν at Rhet. 1365b1-8 governs not 'truth vs. ostentation' but 'reality vs. how-one-appears': πρὸς δόξαν names what one would not choose if escaping notice — i.e. social-appearance, reputation, ethos. δόξα across the Rhetoric is therefore 'opinion/reputation,' not 'ostentation'; Cope's slide from πρὸς δόξαν to 'mere outward show' over-translates. (iv) Reads διδασκαλία at 1404a9 as 'demonstrative practice'; the contrast with geometry is not 'geometry is honest, rhetoric is showy,' but 'geometric proof is πρὸς αὐτόν, rhetorical demonstration is πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν.' The καί at ἅπαντα φαντασία ταῦτ' ἐστὶ καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν is read as adverbial-epexegetic ('I mean phantasia DIRECTED towards the hearer'), not as conjunctive ('and besides directed towards the hearer'); González removes the comma before καί. Phantasia operates in the study of geometry too (per De Mem. 449b30-450a1, νοεῖν οὐκ ἐστιν ἄνευ φαντάσματος); the geometer's phantasia is πρὸς αὐτόν while the orator's is πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν.

section_structure.heading: Phantasia in Aristotle's Oeuvre
section_structure.summary: The article's centerpiece: a sustained survey of phantasia across the Corpus Aristotelicum to show that 'mere show/ostentation' is unparalleled. Traces the suggestion to Freudenthal 1863:17-18, popularized by Nussbaum 1978:254, who proposed it to explain Aristotle's καθάπερ μεταφορά clause at DA 428a1-4. Quotes Wedin 1988:68 confirming that only Rhet. 1404a11 has been adduced for the Freudenthal sense — the reading is one-passage-circular. THE SOPHISTICAL REFUTATIONS PARALLEL — the section's signature move. Halliwell 1993:59 n.16 had glossed phantasia at SE 4 165b25 as 'merely appearance,' chained to 'show.' González rebuts: SE 164a20-21 (οἱ φαινόμενοι ἔλεγχοι) and 164a23-24 (συλλογισμοί, οἳ δ' οὐκ ὄντες δοκοῦσι) make clear that the φαντασία of false reasoning is psychological in character — error from ambiguity (ὁμωνυμία, ἀμφιβολία), wrong disjunction/conjunction, accentuation, similarity of termination — all rooted in aural/visual phantasmata processed by νοῦς. The parallel to DA 428b17-22 (perception of ἴδια vs. αἰσθητά κατὰ συμβεβηκός) and DA 430b29-30 confirms: SE's phantasma-from-distance and DA's perception-at-distance are the same psychological mechanism. Adds Hippocrates Decorum 7 (the other LSJ-cited candidate for 'ostentation' phantasia) is, per Valdés 1992, second-century AD — too late to influence Aristotle. Hdt. 7.10ε φαντάζεσθαι is verbal, not nominal, and its 'ostentation' coloring is strictly contextual. THE POSITIVE ARISTOTELIAN MAP: phantasia as psychic mediator between αἴσθησις and ὑπόληψις (DA 427b14-16); λογιστική vs. αἰσθητική phantasia (DA 433b29-30); βουλευτική φαντασία ἐν τοῖς λογιστικοῖς (DA 434a5-10), which combines πλείω φαντάσματα into one course of action; the De motu animalium causal chain διάνοια/αἴσθησις → φαντασία → ὄρεξις → πάθη (organic-bodily) → motion (700b17-21, 702a17-19); phantasia among the κριτικά faculties; the Rhet. 1370a18-27 division of ἐπιθυμία into ἄλογος and μετὰ λόγου — the latter ἐκ τοῦ πασθῆναι — places aural/rhetorical persuasion squarely in the phantasia-economy. Closes with NE 1102a27-b31 division of the soul (with logos / alogon, the alogon further divided into phytikon and the epithymetikon-orektikon that 'somehow shares in logos').

section_structure.heading: Phantasia in the Rhetoric
section_structure.summary: Closes the argument by mapping all Rhetoric occurrences of phantasia and showing their psychological coherence. The catalog: 1370a28-30 (the famous αἴσθησίς τις ἀσθενής, with τις as a contextual simplification, not a reductive equation); 1370b33 (φαντασία of ὑπεροχή from νίκη); 1371a9 (honor/good repute generate phantasia τοῦ σπουδαῖος εἶναι); 1371a19 (being loved gives phantasia of being good by nature); 1378b10 (dwelling-upon-revenge phantasia); 1382a21 (φόβος as phantasia of future evil); 1383a17 (courage); 1384a22 (αἰσχύνη as phantasia of loss of reputation). In none of these is the emphasis on the unreality of the presented content; the focus is the cognitive process of entertaining the phantasma. The phantasia/doxa distinction at DA 428a20-24 — phantasia does not necessarily carry πίστις, but rhetoric aims to produce phantasia WITH pistis — supplies the rhetorical kernel. Rhet. 1408a16-19 inventory (angry style for hubris, indignant/reticent for impious matters, admiring for praiseworthy, humble for pitiable) is read as construction of visual+aural phantasmata producing 'community of feeling.' Rhet. 1408a19-24: improper lexis makes the audience 'feel-along-with' (συμπαθεῖ) even when the speaker says nothing, because phantasia produces a false inference of truth. Rhet. 1386a29-33: pity-evocation through ἐγγὺς ποιοῦσι φαίνεσθαι via gestures/cries/display/hypokrisis. CLOSING THESIS: lexis works through orator's phantasia → constructed sensory phantasmata (lexis + skhēmata + phōnē) → hearers' sensory phantasmata → hearers' noetic phantasia → ideally pistis-bearing doxa. The 'limit' Aristotle records at 1404a11 (οὐ μέντοι τοσοῦτον) is a realistic estimate of lexis's promise, not a dismissive aside. Proposed retranslation of 1404a8-11 (paraphrastically): lexis has a small but necessary place in every demonstrative discipline, speech-choice makes some difference to clarity though not a large one whose importance should be overstated, and all of this concerns how things will appear to the listener (n.90).

outline: Cluster 1 (pp.99-100, intro): The TAPA SUMMARY frames the article's negative target — the consensus rendering of φαντασία at Rhet. III.1 1404a11 as 'mere show' — and positive thesis: phantasia is 'the psychological function that mediates between sense perception and man's higher intellectual faculties.' On González's reading, Aristotle invokes phantasia to instruct us to read lexis 'against the background of his psychology, as mediating the rhetorical task and entrusted with turning the orator's subject matter into such phantasmata as will successfully shape the opinion of the listeners and gain their pistis.' The opening surveys translations: Cope ('fancy'), Freese ('mere outward show'), Kennedy ('outward show'), Roberts ('fanciful'), Rapp ('reiner Anschein'). Notes that Renaissance scholars (Robortello 1548, Vettori 1579, Barbaro/Barbaro 1544, Riccobono 1588) read the Rhetoric against Aristotle's psychology and gave phantasia 'its full psychological import,' fastening elocutio's role to the species/phantasmata processed by the 'sensitive soul.' Engages Fortenbaugh 2002 — who calls phantasia 'a biological faculty' but still rules a 'psychological' Rhet. III.1 phantasia out of court — by demanding more than the bare equivalence of phantasia and φαίνεσθαι: Fortenbaugh would also have to show that the term occurs in epistemologically unloaded contexts.

Cluster 2 (pp.100-101, intro): Outlines the four-stage strategy. Notes Halliwell 1993:54, 60 in support of the psychological-perceptual reading of 1403b17. Notes Nussbaum 1996:307 on Rh. II.5 fear with the caveat that phantasia at Rh. II is used 'simply as the verbal noun of phainesthai' — González disagrees: pistis cannot exist without doxa (cf. pp.116, 125), and Aristotle elides the possibility of phantasia without doxa in the Rhetoric, which accounts for 'what seems superficially like emotion without belief.' Marks the chiasm between 'phantasia is necessary' (positive psychology) and 'phantasia is potentially abused' (the ethical ambivalence Aristotle records).

Cluster 3 (pp.101-104, S1 opening): Treats the lexis/hypokrisis schema. Construes 1403b18-22 (πρῶτον = pisteis; δεύτερον = lexis; τρίτον = hypokrisis), notes that the consensus reads hypokrisis as a temporary parenthesis closed by Aristotle as he moves to lexis-proper (chapters 2-11), with hypokrisis re-opened only at chapter 12. González: hypokrisis is a subordinate division of lexis, but throughout chapters 2-11 Aristotle continues to attend to delivery (cf. 1403b14-15, returning explicitly to voice and its impact on ethos and pathos). Connects this to the negative reading: if hypokrisis is morally objectionable AND inextricable from lexis, then phantasia, the joint object of both, inherits the moral taint. González denies the moral taint at the source.

Cluster 4 (pp.104-105, S1 close): Quotes in full the 1404a1-12 passage (Greek + Kennedy translation, with Ross 1959 against Kassel 1976 at 1404a2 [οὐχ ὡς ὀρθῶς vs. οὐκ ὀρθῶς] and 1404a4 [ζητεῖν vs. ζητεῖ, μηδὲν πλέον vs. μηδὲν πλείω]). Reads: (i) τῆς πραγματείας τῆς περὶ τὴν ῥητορικήν is πρὸς δόξαν — the WHOLE business of rhetoric, not just hypokrisis. (ii) οὐχ ὡς ὀρθῶς ἔχοντος means 'not because it is right [in an ideal world]' — ὀρθῶς = 'correct/strictly justified,' not 'morally right' (cf. LSJ s.v. ὀρθός III.2; Irwin 1985:391). (iii) The ὥστε-clause renders ἔξω τοῦ ἀποδεῖξαι not 'unjust' but 'περίεργα' = 'superfluous' from the ideal-justice standpoint. (iv) μοχθηρία targets the audience, not the orator: it is the corruption of audience that makes lexis necessary, hence the abuse-potential is symmetric.

Cluster 5 (pp.105-106, S1 continues): Reads ἀλλ' ἅπαντα φαντασία ταῦτ' ἐστὶ καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν. The καί is read as adverbial-epexegetic, not conjunctive: 'I mean phantasia DIRECTED to the hearer.' (See n.42: editors who omit the comma — Bekker, Spengel, Roemer, Kassel, Cope, Sandys — versus Ross and Dufour-Wartelle who insert it.) The διδασκαλία at 1404a9 is glossed not as 'instruction' generically but as 'demonstrative practice' (matching Poetics 1456b5, Plato Gorgias 453d-454e). The διὸ οὐδεὶς οὕτω γεωμετρεῖν διδάσκει is the contrast hinge: geometry proves πρὸς αὑτόν, rhetoric πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν, and phantasia operates in BOTH (De Mem. 449b30 — νοεῖν οὐκ ἐστιν ἄνευ φαντάσματος).

Cluster 6 (pp.106-107, S1 close): The working-definition footnote: Rhet. 1370a28-30 'phantasia is a kind of weak perception (αἴσθησίς τις ἀσθενής), connected with memory and hope.' This is the operative definition for 1404a11. The Stage-1-summary catalogues the reasons for the consensus: μοχθηρία + φορτικόν as ethical condemnation; lexis as ἀναγκαῖος ἐπιμέλεια; the τοσοῦτον limiting clause; the conceptual-clarity-only reading of δηλῶσαι.

Cluster 7 (pp.107-110, S2 opening): Pushes back. The anti-rhetorical pedigree of the consensus is Platonic (Gorgias 463d1-2). Reads μοχθηρία as the ethical cast of any political process: rhetoric addresses the assembly's need to build consensus and manage dissent — hence logos, ethos, and pathos are necessary ingredients, with the symmetric promise of effective democratic governance and the danger of unprincipled exploitation. Reads φορτικότης at 1395b2 (anticipating the φορτικόν of 1403b36): it concerns the pleasure a hearer experiences when an orator hits his preformed opinions. The καλῶς ὑπολαμβανόμενον at 1403b36 is examined in detail: Cope's 'rightly so considered' is challenged with Vettori's 'recte ponderatum' ('when properly considered'). The LSJ entry on ὑπολαμβάνω III.1 'to take up a notion, assume' supports the softer rendering. List of competing modern renderings (Freese, Kennedy, Jebb, Dufour-Wartelle, Rapp, Tovar) is given in n.33.

Cluster 8 (pp.110-111, S2 continues): The Poetics 26 parallel. Aristotle at Poet. 1461b27-29 says 'the lesser is the more vulgar (φορτική), and to such are the lesser audience (θεαταί)' — the φορτική label tracks not the practice but the performer-audience interaction; same for actors/auletai (Poet. 1462a2-6). Mokhthēria and phortikon, in González's reading, both target audience-corruption, not lexis-corruption per se. Therefore lexis (and phantasia, lexis's medium) is not condemned at its root. Side argument (n.34) from Pol. 8.6 1340b20ff on mousike's φορτικότης tracks the same logic.

Cluster 9 (pp.111-112, S2 πρὸς δόξαν): The opposition πρὸς ἀλήθειαν vs. πρὸς δόξαν at Rhet. 1365b1-8 is the key textual lock. Aristotle defines πρὸς δόξαν as 'what one would not choose were one to escape notice' — i.e. matters governed by reputation, social-appearance, ethos. Examples: doing good vs. receiving good (πάσχειν vs. ποιεῖν); being just vs. seeming just; being healthy vs. seeming healthy. Justice 'is a small thing' precisely because it is open to opinion in ways health is not. The judgment is not 'ostentation' but 'reputation-management.' Surveys all Rhetoric occurrences of doxa (1360b22, 1362b20, 1367a17, 1368b23, 1371a16, 1388a2-7, 1404a25, 1372b21-22 etc.) and confirms 'opinion/reputation' as the dominant sense; Rhet. II.1 1377b23-24 anchors the ethos/pathos persona-construction reading.

Cluster 10 (pp.112-113, S2 close): Reads διδασκαλία again and finds the geometry contrast asymmetric: geometric proof, by its nature, is right or wrong for all; rhetorical proof can convince one and fail to convince another. Hence διὸ οὐδεὶς οὕτω γεωμετρεῖν διδάσκει — not 'because geometry is honest and rhetoric showy,' but 'because rhetorical demonstration is πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν.' Footnote 42 on punctuation: the καί is adverbial, marking the directionality of phantasia toward the hearer; editors who insert a comma weaken the immediacy of that directionality. The cluster cites De Mem. 449b30-450a1 (νοεῖν οὐκ ἐστιν ἄνευ φαντάσματος) and 450a4-5 (νοεῖ τίθεται πρὸ ὀμμάτων ποσόν) to anchor phantasia in NON-rhetorical cognition — and conclude that 'mere show' is the wrong gloss.

Cluster 11 (pp.113-115, S3 opening + Freudenthal genealogy): Locates the philological origin of the 'mere show' reading: Freudenthal 1863:17-18 invented it to explain Aristotle's καθάπερ μεταφορά at DA 428a1-4. Nussbaum 1978:254 popularized it — quotes Nussbaum acknowledging the apparent triviality of the move ('It will be objected that this is a trivial point. But for Aristotle it is never trivial to recognize all the senses of a word'). González: the point is trivial; and Wedin 1988:69-70 supplies a better solution to the καθάπερ μεταφορά clause. Wedin 1988:68 explicitly notes that ONLY Rhet. 1404a11 has been adduced for the Freudenthal sense — the reading is circular at the single-passage level.

Cluster 12 (pp.114-115, S3 Sophistical Refutations parallel): THE PIVOTAL MOVE. Halliwell 1993:59 n.16 had glossed phantasia at SE 4 165b25 as 'merely appearance' and pulled this back as a precedent for Rhet. 1404a11. González dissects: SE 165b24-27 lists six sources of false-syllogism appearance — ὁμωνυμία, ἀμφιβολία, σύνθεσις, διαίρεσις, προσῳδία, σχῆμα λέξεως — all of which are psychological phantasia phenomena (false inferences from aurally/visually perceived utterances). The treatise's opening at 164a20-21 (οἱ φαινόμενοι ἔλεγχοι) and 164a23-24 (συλλογισμοί, οἳ δ' οὐκ ὄντες δοκοῦσι) confirms the topic is fallacy-as-phantasia. Aristotle himself draws the parallel at SE 164b27 with 'those who view things from a distance' — the same trope at DA 428b17-22 (perception of ἴδια vs. αἰσθητά κατὰ συμβεβηκός) and DA 430b29-30. Conclusion: SE's phantasia is the psychological faculty, fallible, distance-vulnerable — NOT 'mere show.'

Cluster 13 (p.116, S3 lexical-historical case): The only other LSJ-cited candidate text for 'ostentation' phantasia is [Hippocrates] Decorum 7, which Valdés 1992:304 (in a detailed linguistic study) dates 'with a fair degree of certainty' to the second century AD or later — too late to inform Aristotle. Hdt. 7.10ε φαντάζεσθαι (the only pre-Aristotelian verbal candidate per LSJ φανταζω II.2) is contextually about Artabanos warning Xerxes; God strikes prominent animals (ὑπερέχοντα ζῷα) with thunderbolts, not allowing them 'to show themselves' (φαντάζεσθαι). González: the 'arrogant display' coloring is strictly contextual; this passage does not warrant a lexicon entry, and the verb-to-noun extrapolation is illegitimate (n.57: Martínez Hernández 1997:196 on the distinction between lexical fields and lexical spheres; Coseriu-Geckeler 1981:56-59; Geckeler 1976:158-60).

Cluster 14 (pp.117-119, S3 positive Aristotelian map): Sets out the conceptual scaffolding for the psychological phantasia. DA 427b14-16: phantasia is distinct from both αἴσθησις and διάνοια but does not occur without αἴσθησις; ὑπόληψις cannot occur without phantasia. DA 433b27-30: animal motion presupposes ὄρεξις, which presupposes phantasia, which can be λογιστική or αἰσθητική. DA 434a5-10: βουλευτικὴ φαντασία ἐν τοῖς λογιστικοῖς combines πλείω φαντάσματα into one. González reads βουλευτική not as 'imagination preexisting deliberation' but as 'imagination connected with deliberation' (following Wedin 1988:82-83); deliberation may either presuppose or actively craft the phantasmata. DA 431b6-8 anchors logistika and bouleutika phantasmata.

Cluster 15 (pp.119-120, S3 De motu animalium chain): De motu an. 702a17-19: τὰ μὲν γὰρ ὀργανικὰ μέρη παρασκευάζει ἐπιτηδείως τὰ πάθη, ἡ δ' ὄρεξις τὰ πάθη, τὴν δ' ὄρεξιν ἡ φαντασία. αὕτη δὲ γίνεται ἢ διὰ νοήσεως ἢ δι' αἰσθήσεως. The causal chain: thought-or-sense-perception → phantasia → desire → bodily affections → motion. Crucial distinction: the πάθη of this chain are bodily (chillings/heatings, per Nussbaum 1978:154 n.19), not psychic affections; the psychic πάθη of Rhetoric II precede desire and motivate judgment/action. De motu an. 700b17-21: phantasia and αἴσθησις occupy the SAME place as νοῦς, since all are κριτικά. González reads this to underwrite phantasia's role in rhetorical κρίσις (Rhet. 1355a22-23 + 1377b20-22 on rhetoric as ἕνεκα κρίσεως).

Cluster 16 (pp.121-122, S3 close): The soul's two parts (NE 1102a27-28): λόγον ἔχον and ἄλογον. The first further divides into ἐπιστημονικόν and λογιστικόν (NE 1139a3-8). Aristotle/Plato comparison: Aristotle places desire in the sphere of logos and so makes it 'object of persuasion and rational appeal.' Rhet. 1370a18-27: ἐπιθυμία divides into ἄλογος and μετὰ λόγου; the latter is ἐκ τοῦ πασθῆναι: 'they often long to see and acquire when they have heard and been persuaded' (ἀκούσαντες καὶ πεισθέντες). González reads ἀκούσαντες-πεισθέντες as conceptually subordinated (not coordinated), illustrating that rhetorical persuasion is preeminently oral-aural and that, contra Fortenbaugh 2002:100, the De Anima / Rhetoric cleavage cannot be drawn on the phantasia/doxa distinction (which Aristotle elides in the Rhetoric because rhetorical phantasia carries pistis).

Cluster 17 (pp.122-125, S4 Rhetoric inventory): Catalogs all phantasia occurrences in the Rhetoric and shows their psychological coherence. (i) 1370a28-30: φαντασία ἐστὶν αἴσθησίς τις ἀσθενής — the τις signals a contextual simplification ('a sort of weak perception'), not an ontological reduction. Watson 1982:103 n.6 and Wedin 1988:89 agree. (ii) 1370b33: phantasia of ὑπεροχή from νίκη. (iii) 1371a9: honor's pleasure consists in phantasia τοῦ σπουδαῖος εἶναι. (iv) 1371a19: being loved produces phantasia of being-good-by-nature. (v) 1378b10: revenge-phantasia. (vi) 1382a21, 1383a17, 1384a22: phobos as phantasia of future evil; courage; aischynē as phantasia of loss of reputation. In NONE of these is the emphasis on unreality; the emphasis is on the cognitive process. González develops a fine theoretical distinction here: in Rhet. 1370a27-28 ἐν τῷ αἰσθάνεσθαί τινος πάθους — πάθος here covers anything that comes ἐκ τοῦ πάσχειν: emotions, but also states of mind and body (sleep, memory, phantasmata themselves per De Mem. 450a10-11).

Cluster 18 (pp.125-126, S4 doxa/pistis distinction): DA 428a20-24 distinguishes phantasia from doxa: phantasia does not necessarily carry πίστις. González reads this as the rhetorical kernel — pistis is the goal of rhetoric, but phantasia is its substrate; the orator's task is to transform phantasia into pistis-bearing doxa. The rhetorical art accordingly works at all cognitive levels (including the πίστεις inherent in αὐτὰ τὰ πράγματα), but pertains especially to pathos: 'Even a speaker's successful self-presentation, which turns on his ability to communicate proper ethos, can be reinterpreted as phantasia towards the hearers with a view to creating such πάθη as will move them to act to the speaker's advantage.'

Cluster 19 (pp.126-127, S4 lexis-skhēmata-phōnē): Rhet. 1408a16-19 (the orator chooses 'angry style' for hubris, 'indignant/reticent' for impious matters, 'admiring' for praiseworthy, 'humble' for pitiable). These are 'all matters of style and delivery,' requiring intonation/loudness/prose-rhythm choices and a fitting countenance (1408b4-7). Rhet. 1408a19-24: 'the proper lexis also makes the matter credible: the mind draws a false inference of the truth of what a speaker says because they feel the same about such things, so they think the facts to be so, even if they are not as the speaker represents them; and the hearer suffers along with the pathetic speaker, even if what he says amounts to nothing.' González reads the κἂν μηδὲν λέγῃ not as condoning deception but as observing that rhetoric is open to manipulation — phantasia's symmetric promise/danger.

Cluster 20 (pp.127-128, S4 close + Poetics 17 parallel): Rhet. 1386a29-33 + 1386a33-34: pity-evocation through ἐγγὺς ποιοῦσι φαίνεσθαι via gestures (σχήμασιν), cries (φωναῖς), display of feeling, and generally ὑπόκρισις. Poetics 17 1455a22-32: the poet should 'put-before-eyes' (πρὸ ὀμμάτων τιθέμενον) and 'work-himself-into-grief-with-the-action' (τῇ λέξει συναπεργαζόμενον). Conclusion: lexis-as-phantasia is the orator's craft of converting his own internal [re]presentation into hearers' phantasmata, which becomes hearers' phantasia, which (ideally) carries pistis and so becomes hearers' doxa. The 'limit' Aristotle records at 1404a11 (οὐ μέντοι τοσοῦτον) is the realistic estimate of lexis's promise. Proposed retranslation (paraphrastically): lexis has a small but necessary place in every demonstrative discipline; speech-choice makes some difference to clarity but not a great one; all of it concerns how things appear to the listener (n.90).

concepts.label: Phantasia as psychological mediator (not 'mere show')
concepts.summary: González's signature thesis: phantasia in Rhet. III.1 1404a11 is the SAME psychological function described in De Anima — the mediating faculty between αἴσθησις and the higher cognitive faculties (ὑπόληψις, doxa, νοῦς, βούλευσις). Not 'mere outward show,' not 'ostentation,' not 'fancy.' The reading is licensed by Aristotle's own uniform usage across 100+ occurrences of the noun in his oeuvre, and by the linguistic-historical fact that the 'ostentation' sense of φαντασία appears only in late authors (Polybius and after; Hippocrates Decorum 7 is post-Aristotelian per Valdés 1992).

concepts.label: Rhetorical phantasia is psychological, not sophistic deception
concepts.summary: Halliwell 1993:59 n.16 had cited SE 4 165b25 as a parallel for an allegedly non-psychological, 'merely appearance' phantasia. González: the SE phantasia IS psychological — it names the perceptual-cognitive mechanism by which fallacies (φαινόμενοι ἔλεγχοι, SE 164a20-21) appear as syllogisms when they are not (συλλογισμοί, οἳ δ' οὐκ ὄντες δοκοῦσι, SE 164a23-24). The Rhet. III.1 phantasia is not Sophistic deception precisely because it is the SAME faculty; it is rhetorically legitimate when not detached from ethical/dialectical grounding.

concepts.label: The καί at 1404a11 as adverbial-epexegetic, not conjunctive
concepts.summary: González's textual-critical claim: in ἀλλ' ἅπαντα φαντασία ταῦτ' ἐστὶ καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν, the καί is adverbial ('I mean phantasia DIRECTED towards the hearer'), not conjunctive ('and ALSO directed towards the hearer'). The translation difference is non-trivial: the conjunctive reading underwrites 'mere show + directed at the hearer'; the adverbial reading underwrites 'phantasia, that is, the kind directed at the hearer.' Editors removing the comma (Bekker, Spengel, Roemer, Kassel, Cope, Sandys) implicitly support González; those inserting it (Ross, Dufour-Wartelle) implicitly support the consensus.

concepts.label: Hypokrisis as subordinate-not-parenthetical division of lexis
concepts.summary: Against the consensus that reads hypokrisis as a temporary parenthesis Aristotle closes when he moves to lexis-proper (chapters 2-11), González argues that hypokrisis is a SUBORDINATE division of lexis that Aristotle continues to track throughout chapters 2-11. This matters because the negative reading of phantasia depends on phantasia inheriting the moral taint of hypokrisis; if hypokrisis is not morally tainted at the root (only abusable), then phantasia is not tainted either.

concepts.label: πρὸς δόξαν as reputation-management, not ostentation
concepts.summary: Rhet. 1365b1-8: πρὸς δόξαν = 'what one would not choose were one to escape notice.' This names reputation, social-appearance, ethos-management — not 'ostentation' or 'mere outward show.' Cope's slide from πρὸς δόξαν to 'ostentatious and hollow' over-translates. The Eudemian Ethics 1215a29-30 parallel (φορτικὰς τέχνας τὰς πρὸς δόξαν πραγματευομένας μόνον) does not license the slide either: Rackham's LCL renders it neutrally 'pursued only for reputation.'

concepts.label: διδασκαλία at 1404a9 as demonstrative practice
concepts.summary: Aristotle at 1404a9 says lexis has a small necessary place ἐν πάσῃ διδασκαλίᾳ. González reads διδασκαλία not as 'instruction' generically but as 'demonstrative practice' — the practice common to rhetorical proof and geometric proof. The geometer/rhetorician contrast is then NOT 'honest geometry vs. showy rhetoric' but 'geometric demonstration πρὸς αὑτόν vs. rhetorical demonstration πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν.' Phantasia operates in BOTH (De Mem. 449b30-450a1).

concepts.label: Phantasia as 'sort of weak perception' (1370a28-30)
concepts.summary: Aristotle's working definition: φαντασία ἐστὶν αἴσθησίς τις ἀσθενής, connected with memory and hope. The τις is a contextual hedge marking an approximation; it does not collapse phantasia into perception. Phantasia 'attends' memory and hope just as it 'attends' present perception.

concepts.label: Bouleutikē phantasia as image-combining capacity
concepts.summary: DA 434a5-10: ἡ βουλευτικὴ [φαντασία] ἐν τοῖς λογιστικοῖς — the rational animal can, ἐκ πλειόνων φαντασμάτων, fashion one course of action by measuring against a single standard (the greater good). González uses this to bridge psychological phantasia and rhetorical practice: the orator artfully crafts phantasmata that will prompt the audience's deliberative combination toward the desired krisis.

concepts.label: De motu causal chain (thought/perception → phantasia → desire → bodily pathē → motion)
concepts.summary: De motu an. 702a17-19 + 700b17-21: phantasia mediates between sense-perception/thought and desire/motion. CRITICAL: the πάθη of De motu's chain are BODILY (chillings/heatings); the psychic πάθη of Rhetoric II are NOT in that chain — they precede desire and motivate judgment/action.

concepts.label: Phantasia + pistis = rhetorical goal
concepts.summary: DA 428a20-24 distinguishes phantasia from doxa: phantasia does NOT necessarily carry πίστις. González's elegant resolution: rhetoric's goal is precisely phantasia-WITH-pistis. The orator works to make the audience's phantasia carry the conviction of doxa. In the Rhetoric Aristotle elides the possibility of phantasia without doxa (cf. nn.6, 53), explaining what to Nussbaum 1996:321 n.16 looks like 'emotion without belief.'

concepts.label: Logistikē vs. aisthētikē phantasia (DA 433b29-30)
concepts.summary: Phantasia divides into λογιστική (connected with logos) and αἰσθητική (connected with sense-perception alone, shared with non-rational animals). The disjunctive ἢ … ἢ need not be exclusive: the logistikē may still ultimately be aisthēsis-grounded (DA 432a3-10; Wedin 1988:114; Labarrière 1984:47 n.32). Rhetoric, as a logos-bearing art directed at logos-bearing humans, works with logistikē phantasia.

concepts.label: Mokhthēria and phortikon track audience-interaction, not lexis-itself
concepts.summary: Drawing the Poetics 26 parallel (1461b27-29; 1462a2-6): φορτική as a label tracks the performer-audience interaction, not the inherent character of the practice. Mokhthēria and phortikon are properties of corrupt audiences (and the orators who pander to them), not properties of lexis or phantasia as such.

concepts.label: Emotions as definitionally phantasiai
concepts.summary: Rhet. 1382a21 (φόβος = phantasia of future evil); 1383a17 (courage); 1384a22 (αἰσχύνη = phantasia of loss of reputation). Emotions are not 'irrational' affections but cognitive engagements with phantasmata. Lexis works on emotions because lexis produces phantasmata.

concepts.label: Rhetorical task as phantasma-construction
concepts.summary: The orator turns his own phantasia (internal [re]presentations) into sensory phantasmata (lexis + skhēmata + phōnē) that the audience receives via their senses, processes into their own phantasia, and ideally accepts with pistis — i.e., as doxa. This is the rhetorical economy of phantasia.

concepts.label: Logos as oratio (speech), not just ratio (reason)
concepts.summary: Per Labarrière 1984 (n.83): phantasia connects via phone (GA 786b23-25; DA 420b29-33) to αἰσθητική phantasia, and phone is the σημεῖον of pain/pleasure (Pol. 1253a10-11). The logos of rhetoric is preeminently oratio — the spoken word — and so phantasia in the Rhetoric is the auditor's response to spoken-and-heard phantasmata.

concepts.label: Geometer's phantasia πρὸς αὑτόν vs. orator's phantasia πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν
concepts.summary: The geometry/rhetoric contrast at 1404a12 is not about honesty vs. showiness but about the directionality of demonstration. Geometric proof is πρὸς αὑτόν (the proof works for one and all by its own logic); rhetorical demonstration is πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν (it must convince a particular hearer). Phantasia operates in both, differently directed.

concepts.label: Phantasia as a kritikon faculty
concepts.summary: De motu an. 700b17-21: phantasia and αἴσθησις occupy the SAME place as νοῦς, since πάντα κριτικά. Phantasia participates in judgment-making, and so in rhetoric's ἕνεκα κρίσεως goal (Rhet. 1377b20-22).

concepts.label: Freudenthal-Nussbaum genealogy of the 'mere show' reading
concepts.summary: González's philological-historical claim: the 'mere show' reading goes back to Freudenthal 1863:17-18 (proposed to handle DA 428a1-4 καθάπερ μεταφορά). Nussbaum 1978:254 popularized it. Wedin 1988:68 acknowledges that Rhet. 1404a11 is the SOLE Aristotelian passage adduced for the Freudenthal sense — making the textual evidence one-passage-circular.

concepts.label: Hypolēpsis without phantasia is impossible (DA 427b14-16)
concepts.summary: DA 427b14-16: phantasia is distinct from αἴσθησις and διάνοια, never occurs without αἴσθησις, AND ὑπόληψις never occurs without phantasia. Therefore phantasia is constitutive of the very faculty by which rhetorical kriseis are formed.

concepts.label: Pathos at 1370a28 in the broad sense ('what is undergone')
concepts.summary: πάθος in αἰσθάνεσθαί τινος πάθους covers anything that comes ἐκ τοῦ πάσχειν — emotions, but also bodily states (sleep, De Insomn. 462a3-4), memory (De Mem. 449b4-6), and phantasmata themselves (De Mem. 450a10-11). The αἴσθησις-πάθος-φαντασία triangulation undergirds the 'sort of weak perception' definition.

readings.label: Psychological-phantasia thesis: Rhet. III.1 1404a11 phantasia is the De Anima faculty, NOT 'mere show'
readings.summary: González's central reading: the phantasia of Rhet. III.1 1404a11 is the same psychological function described in De Anima — mediating between sense-perception and the higher cognitive faculties (memory, hope, doxa, hypolēpsis). The 'mere outward show' rendering (Cope, Freese, Kennedy, Roberts, Rapp) is corrected. Defended on three grounds: (a) Aristotle's 100+ uses of the noun phantasia in his oeuvre yield no instance for which 'ostentation' is required; (b) the linguistic-historical record shows 'ostentation' only in late authors (Polybius and after); (c) the contextual interpretation of 1404a1-12 — once mokhthēria, phortikon, and πρὸς δόξαν are correctly construed — does not require the pejorative gloss. The reading is anchored in 1370a28-30 (phantasia as αἴσθησίς τις ἀσθενής) and the systematic survey of Rhetoric occurrences.

readings.label: Sophistical Refutations parallel rescues phantasia from 'mere show'
readings.summary: González's SIGNATURE philological move: SE 4 165b24-27 + 164a20-24 list the sources of false-syllogism appearance — ὁμωνυμία, ἀμφιβολία, σύνθεσις, διαίρεσις, προσῳδία, σχῆμα λέξεως — all of which are psychological phantasia phenomena (false inferences from aurally/visually perceived utterances). Halliwell 1993:59 n.16 had cited SE 165b25 as a precedent for non-psychological 'mere appearance' phantasia at Rhet. 1404a11; González inverts the inference: the SE phantasia is precisely the same psychological faculty, fallible and vulnerable to distance/ambiguity (DA 428b17-22, 430b29-30). The Rhet. III.1 phantasia is therefore not Sophistic deception, but the legitimate psychological substrate of any rhetorical-OR-fallacious appearance. González also documents that the only other LSJ-cited candidate for 'ostentation' phantasia ([Hippocrates] Decorum 7) is post-Aristotelian (Valdés 1992) and that Hdt. 7.10ε's φαντάζεσθαι is verbal-contextual, not a license for the noun.

readings.label: Correction of the Kennedy/English-reading translation tradition
readings.summary: González methodically catalogs and corrects the English-language translation tradition on phantasia at 1404a11. Cope 1877: 'fancy'/'the mental presentation, a mere copy, without reality.' Freese 1926: 'mere outward show.' Roberts in Ross 1924: 'fanciful.' Kennedy 1991: 'outward show.' Rapp 2002: 'reiner Anschein.' Tovar 1953 and Jebb in Sandys 1909 are slightly more cautious ('apariencia,' 'imagination'). The proposed retranslation: 'Nevertheless, the subject of lexis has some small necessary place in every demonstrative discipline, for speaking this way or that makes some difference to getting across clearly; yet not so great a difference — its importance should not be overstated — but all this is a matter of how things will appear to the listener.' This rendering preserves Aristotle's psychological commitments and the realistic-estimate function of τοσοῦτον.

readings.label: Phantasia-with-pistis as the rhetorical goal
readings.summary: The orator's rhetorical task is to convert phantasia (which, per DA 428a20-24, does not by itself carry pistis) into pistis-bearing phantasia, i.e., into doxa. The orator works at all the available cognitive levels: pisteis inherent in αὐτὰ τὰ πράγματα (where the geometer too uses phantasmata), but especially at the level of pathos. The orator turns his own phantasia (internal [re]presentation) into sensory phantasmata (lexis + skhēmata + phōnē); these become hearers' sensory phantasmata; these become hearers' noetic phantasia; this, supported by lexis-induced pathos, comes to carry pistis and so becomes the hearers' own doxa. Lexis-as-phantasia is the orator's craft of phantasma-construction. The 'limit' Aristotle records at 1404a11 (οὐ μέντοι τοσοῦτον) is the realistic estimate of lexis's promise, not a dismissive aside.

readings.label: Hypokrisis as substantive, not parenthetical
readings.summary: Against the consensus that reads hypokrisis as morally objectionable and a temporary parenthesis closed when Aristotle turns to lexis-proper, González argues that hypokrisis is a SUBORDINATE division of lexis tracked throughout chapters 2-11 (continuing attention to voice and its impact on ethos/pathos at multiple points). The negative reading of phantasia depended on phantasia inheriting hypokrisis's moral taint; if hypokrisis is not tainted at the root (only abusable, in the manner of any rhetorical resource), then phantasia is not tainted either.

greek_terms.summary: Central term. González argues phantasia in Rhet. III.1 1404a11 is the same psychological faculty described in De Anima — mediating between αἴσθησις and the higher cognitive faculties (ὑπόληψις, doxa, νοῦς, βούλευσις). NOT 'mere outward show.' Operative definition at Rhet. 1370a28-30: αἴσθησίς τις ἀσθενής, connected with memory and hope.
The product of phantasia. DA 431a14-15: τὰ φαντάσματα οἷον αἰσθήματα ὑπάρχει for the διανοητικὴ ψυχή. The orator constructs phantasmata that become the listeners' phantasia.
Verbal cognate. Hdt. 7.10ε is the sole pre-Aristotelian candidate for 'arrogant display' coloring — González: strictly contextual, not lexicalized.

Verbal stem related to phantasia. Aristotle's φανῆναι at Rhet. 1403b17 is read as deliberate signaling of the psychology of perception. φαινόμενοι ἔλεγχοι at SE 164a20-21 names the fallacy-as-phantasia phenomenon.
The subject of Rhetoric III. González reads lexis at 1404a11 broadly: τὸ περὶ τὴν λέξιν includes hypokrisis as a subordinate division. Lexis is the rhetorical medium that produces phantasmata.
'Lies in the voice' (Rhet. 1403b27-28). Subordinate division of lexis, NOT a temporary parenthesis. Not morally objectionable at its root — only abusable.

Rhetoric is wholly πρὸς δόξαν. Survey of Rhetoric occurrences yields 'opinion/reputation' as dominant sense, not 'ostentation.' DA 428a20-24: phantasia and doxa distinct — phantasia does not necessarily carry πίστις.
Rhetoric's goal is phantasia-WITH-pistis. Plural pisteis = the three rhetorical proofs (logos/ethos/pathos). Pistis attends doxa but not always phantasia (DA 428a20-24).
Phantasia mediates between aisthēsis and higher cognitive faculties. αἴσθησίς τις ἀσθενής is the operative definition. Phantasia never occurs without aisthēsis (DA 427b14-16).

The higher cognitive faculty. Renaissance commentators articulated 'the relationship between mens (νοῦς) and animus (θυμός) on the fulcrum of phantasia.' DA 431a16-17: οὐδέποτε νοεῖ ἄνευ φαντάσματος ἡ ψυχή.
DA 427b14-16: ὑπόληψις never occurs without phantasia. Phantasia is constitutive of the very faculty by which rhetorical kriseis are formed.
DA 433b27-30: animal motion presupposes ὄρεξις, which presupposes phantasia. The De motu causal chain: thought/perception → phantasia → orexis → bodily pathē → motion.

Broad sense: anything from πάσχειν — emotions, bodily states (sleep, memory, phantasmata). The pathē of De motu are bodily; the psychic pathē of Rhetoric II precede desire and motivate judgment. Emotions are phantasiai (Rhet. 1382a21, 1384a22).

One of the three rhetorical proofs. González: a speaker's ethos-construction is reinterpretable as 'phantasia toward the hearers with a view to creating pathē.' Hence ethos and pathos overlap, contra Fortenbaugh 1996.
Rhetoric is ἕνεκα κρίσεως (Rhet. 1377b20-22). Phantasia is a κριτικόν faculty (De motu an. 700b17-21) — occupies the same place as νοῦς in soul-mapping.
DA 434a5-10: the rational animal can ἐκ πλειόνων φαντασμάτων combine one course of action. The orator's craft activates the listeners' bouleutikē phantasia.
DA 433b29-30. The rhetorical-art works with logistikē, but via phōnē + skhēmata accesses aisthētikē in audiences (Labarrière 1984).
Rhet. 1404a8. González: targets the audience, not lexis or phantasia. Mokhthēria τῶν ἀκροατῶν is the conditioning fact that makes lexis 'necessary.'

Rhet. 1403b36 + 1395b2. González reads as a label tracking performer-audience interaction (per Poetics 26 parallel at 1461b27-29), not inherent in lexis/phantasia. The καλῶς ὑπολαμβανόμενον qualifier is read in Vettori's sense ('when properly understood'), not Cope's ('rightly so considered').

Rhet. 1404a9. González reads as 'demonstrative practice' (mathematics-like) — the practice common to rhetoric and geometry. Phantasia operates in both, but with different directionality (πρὸς αὑτόν vs. πρὸς τὸν ἀκροατήν).
Rhet. 1404a6. Narrow sense: enthymematic demonstration (pragma/logos). Outside ἀπόδειξις is περίεργα from the ideal-justice standpoint.
Rhet. 1404a7. The ὥστε-clause renders τἄλλα ἔξω τοῦ ἀποδεῖξαι not 'unjust' but 'superfluous from the ideal-justice standpoint.' Crucial for the consensus-correction.
Hypokrisis ἐν τῇ φωνῇ (1403b27-28). Phōnē as σημεῖον of pleasure/pain (Pol. 1253a10-11). Bridge between αἰσθητική phantasia and rhetorical practice (Labarrière).
Visual phantasma-producers in delivery. Rhet. 1386a31: pity-evocation via σχήμασιν. Also σχῆμα λέξεως at SE 165b27 — fallacy-source.

Rhet. 1386a31, 1386a33-34: speakers make the evil appear ἐγγὺς through visualizing operations. Poetics 17 1455a23: πρὸ ὀμμάτων τιθέμενον. The rhetorical phantasma-construction technique par excellence.

greek_terms.term: homōnumia / amphibolia / sunthesis / dihairesis / prosōdia / skhēma lexeōs
greek_terms.summary: SE 165b24-27: six sources of false-syllogism phantasia. All grounded in aural/visual phantasmata. González uses this catalog to rebut Halliwell's 'merely appearance' reading of SE phantasia.
Rhet. 1370a28-30: phantasia connected with both memory and ἐλπίζειν. Fear and courage as phantasiai of future evil/safety (1382a21, 1383a17).
Rhet. 1370a28-30: phantasia attends memory. De Mem. 449b4-6: mnēmē as pathos.

greek_terms.term: idia (aisthēta) vs. koina vs. kata sumbebēkos
greek_terms.summary: DA II.6 418a20-24 + 428b17-22 + 430b29-30. Proper sensibles infallible; incidental aisthēta (the white-thing-as-Diares's-son) fallible. The double-sidedness of perception grounds αἰσθητική phantasia.
De motu causal chain features phantasia as KINETIC mediator. Not González's focus terminologically but conceptually load-bearing.

tensions.label: Lexis as 'necessary expedient' (ἀναγκαῖος) yet ideally superfluous (περίεργα)
tensions.summary: Rhet. 1404a2-7: δίκαιον is contending αὐτοῖς τοῖς πράγμασιν, and τἄλλα ἔξω τοῦ ἀποδεῖξαι are περίεργα. Yet lexis 'has a small necessary place in every διδασκαλία.' The tension is ethical-pragmatic, not ethical-deceptive. González's resolution: lexis is necessary because of audience mokhthēria, not because rhetoric is constitutively dishonest. The 'superfluous' is from the ideal-justice standpoint; in the actual polis, lexis is required.

tensions.label: Phantasia without pistis (DA 428a20-24) vs. Rhetoric's elision of that possibility
tensions.summary: DA distinguishes phantasia (which need not carry πίστις) from doxa (which does). Rhetoric, however, treats phantasia as if always pistis-bearing (e.g. emotions defined as phantasiai with full motivational force). González: Aristotle elides the DA-distinction in the Rhetoric because the rhetorical goal is precisely phantasia-with-pistis. This solves Nussbaum 1996:321 n.16's puzzle about 'emotion without belief.'

tensions.label: Hypokrisis as parenthetical excursus (consensus) vs. subordinate division of lexis (González)
tensions.summary: The standard view reads hypokrisis as a temporary subject closed at the end of Rhet. III.1 and reopened only at III.12. González argues that hypokrisis is throughout chapters 2-11 as a subordinate division of lexis — Aristotle continues to attend to voice and ethos/pathos delivery. The textual stakes: if hypokrisis is parenthetical-and-objectionable, phantasia inherits the taint; if hypokrisis is subordinate-and-legitimate, phantasia is rescued.

tensions.label: Freudenthal's verb-to-noun extrapolation vs. Aristotle's 100+ noun-uses
tensions.summary: Freudenthal 1863 inferred 'ostentation' for phantasia at DA 428a1-4 (and by extension Rhet. 1404a11) by analogy from Hdt. 7.10ε φαντάζεσθαι. González (with Wedin 1988:68): the noun phantasia in Aristotle's oeuvre never elsewhere means 'ostentation'; 'mere show' is a one-passage extrapolation lacking the verb/noun and synchronic/diachronic-lexical warrant (Martínez Hernández 1997; Coseriu-Geckeler 1981; Geckeler 1976; Gutiérrez Ordóñez 1989).

tensions.label: Fortenbaugh's DA/Rhetoric cleavage vs. González's continuity-thesis
tensions.summary: Fortenbaugh 2002:96-100 calls phantasia a 'biological faculty' (DA) but denies a 'scientific' phantasia-account in the Rhetoric. González: the verb-noun distinction matters (φαίνεσθαι can be colloquial; phantasia as a noun resists colloquial-only readings), and Aristotle's epistemological investment in phantasia (DA 427b14-16, 428a20-24) carries into the Rhetoric. The DA/Rhetoric cleavage cannot be drawn on the phantasia/doxa distinction (which the Rhetoric elides).

tensions.label: Fortenbaugh's ethos/pathos separation vs. González's overlap-thesis
tensions.summary: Fortenbaugh 1996 argues persuasion through character is not intended to arouse emotion, citing NE 1166b30-35's eunoia/philia distinction. González: even if NE distinguishes them, Athenian orators routinely manifested intense philia for their city (cf. Aristoph. Knights 732, 773, 1339-55); ethos-construction generates eunoia and warm-feeling toward the speaker. Carey 1994:35, Russell 1990:205-6 anchor the overlap-reading.

tensions.label: Adverbial καί (González) vs. conjunctive καί (consensus) at 1404a11
tensions.summary: The textual-philological micro-question that drives the larger interpretation. Adverbial-epexegetic reading: 'I mean phantasia DIRECTED to the hearer.' Conjunctive reading: 'all this is phantasia, AND directed to the hearer.' Editors' punctuation choices (Bekker/Spengel/Roemer/Kassel/Cope/Sandys vs. Ross/Dufour-Wartelle) implicitly take sides without flagging the philological stake.

comparison_paragraph: The two papers in the cluster most clearly in dialogue with González are O'Gorman (PHX-05, 2005) and Hawhee (PHX-07, 2011), the other rhetoric-cluster pieces. Hawhee, writing five years later, explicitly registers González 2006 as 'an important exception' in her Note 16 — locating González as the corrective to the (Kennedy-mediated) English-reading tradition that read phantasia in Rhet. III.1 pejoratively. O'Gorman, writing in parallel (Phil&Rhet 38.1, 2005), shares González's foundational impulse — to take phantasia in the Rhetoric seriously as a psychological-rhetorical category — but pursues a different textual strategy: where González focuses tightly on the single passage 1404a11 and rebuilds the philological-lexicographical case for a psychological reading, O'Gorman ranges across Rhetoric I.3 (theōros), I.9 (epideictic-amplification, megethos), II (emotions-as-phantasiai), and III (lexis-as-phantasia), arguing for phantasia's rhetorical home in the EPIDEICTIC function. The two papers are methodologically complementary: González supplies the textual-lock at 1404a11; O'Gorman supplies the wide-angle rhetorical-economy that explains why that lock matters. Both reject the Sorabji/Cope/Kennedy image-and-show consensus; both endorse the Nussbaum-broadening of phantasia (though González is more critical of Nussbaum 1978 specifically for popularizing Freudenthal's reading); both treat the lexis-phantasia conjunction as the textual bridge between Rhet. and DA. Methodological differences: González is a philologist-philosopher engaging Renaissance commentary (Vettori, Robortello, Riccobono, Barbaro) and the modern editorial-textual tradition (Bekker, Spengel, Roemer, Kassel, Ross); O'Gorman is a rhetorician engaging post-1970s rhetoric scholarship (Schiappa, Walker, Lanham, Rosenfield, Hauser, Sullivan). The philological vs. rhetorical-theoretical division of labor is striking and productive. With Nussbaum (PHX-01), González is more critical than O'Gorman: where O'Gorman endorses Nussbaum's broadening at face value, González traces a problematic Freudenthal-Nussbaum genealogy and argues that Nussbaum's 1978 popularization of 'mere show' (motivated by DA 428a1-4 καθάπερ μεταφορά) misled subsequent translators. Yet González still uses Nussbaum's De motu translation at key points. With Frede (PHX-03), González is courteous but not deeply engaged — Frede's supervenience thesis is broadly compatible with González's mediating-faculty reading but operates at a different level of abstraction. With White (PHX-02) and Caston (PHX-04), González does NOT engage, which is a notable cluster-citation gap. On the rhetoric side, the cluster's payoff is: (a) Nussbaum-1985's broadening of phantasia (PHX-01) gets weaponized differently by O'Gorman 2005 (epideictic-amplification application), González 2006 (psychological-mediation philological correction), and Hawhee 2011 (rhetorical-vision generalization across Rhet. I/II/III). (b) The translation history Kennedy 1991 / Freese 1926 / Cope 1877 is, after González, untenable; Newman 2002, González 2006, and Hawhee 2011 together rebuild Aristotle's rhetorical-phantasia as a serious psychological-rhetorical category. (c) The cluster's debate on phantasia's rhetorical home (style-only at III.1 vs. epideictic-amplification vs. cross-corpus rhetorical-vision) is the rhetoric-side scholarly trajectory the cluster maps. González's specific contribution is the textual-critical-philological foundation. Cross-pipeline bridges: (i) BCAP / Heidegger GA 18 1924 Marburg lectures on Aristotle's Rhetoric — Heidegger reads phantasia in DA + Rhet. in tandem with NE — González's psychological-reading mirrors Heidegger's psychological-existential reading at structural level. (ii) Aristotle pipeline — every Bekker locus González cites (Rhet., DA, De Mem., De Motu An., NE, Poet., SE, Pol., GA) feeds the Aristotelian KU map directly. (iii) Dalton dissertation chapters on rhetorical phantasia — González's psychological-mediation reading anchors any chapter treating Rhet. III.1 1404a11 phantasia.
